**The Ordinary Miracle**

The most ordinary miracle I know is language. Consider what's happening right now: I'm arranging symbols, and if I do it well, something will happen inside your mind that approximates something that happened inside mine. Not perfectly—never perfectly—but close enough that for a moment we might be thinking adjacent thoughts.

There's no physical mechanism for this transfer. No wire runs between us. The words are just pressure waves in air or pixels on a screen, and yet entire worlds travel through them. Someone dead for four hundred years can make you laugh. Someone on the other side of the planet can break your heart. A recipe can carry a grandmother's hands across decades into your kitchen tonight.

What moves me most is the generosity embedded in it all. Every word was built by people trying to reach each other. "Serendipity" exists because someone wanted to name a specific kind of lucky accident. "Saudade," "toska," "hiraeth"—whole vocabularies invented because humans refused to let certain feelings go unnamed. Language is a massive, collaborative act of care, assembled across millennia by people who mostly never met.

And it's unfinished. Right now, someone is coining a phrase that will outlive them. Somewhere, two friends are inventing a private joke that will become, for them, a word.

We rarely notice any of this. Language works best when it's invisible, like glass. But every so often I catch myself mid-sentence and feel astonished that it works at all.
